name: Kop
description: Kop (also known as Cop) is a traditional Polish trick-taking game that is a cultural staple of the Greater Poland (Wielkopolska) region. Played with a highly condensed 16-card deck, it is celebrated for its extreme speed and complex partnership dynamics. history.origins: Developed from the German Schafkopf game in the 19th century, Kop was adapted by Polish players in regions under Prussian influence. It became a distinct Polish identity game through the inclusion of the 'Wedding' (Wesele) contract.
timeline: Late 1800s: Schafkopf variants evolve into the 16-card Kop in PoznaÅ„.
1950s: Becomes a standard pub game across Greater Poland.
2012: The Grand Prix of Poland in Kop is established.
Present: Very popular in tournaments; standardized rules enforced by several regional associations.
history.cultural: The game's terminology (Wesele, Zolo, Kontra) is a mix of Polish and German, reflecting the region's complex history.
history.evolution: The game's evolution focused on maximizing the number of trumps (14 out of 16), creating a game where side-suit play is nearly non-existent.

setup.players: 4 players playing in partnerships or solo depending on the contract.
setup.deck: 16 French-suited cards: Ace, 10, Queen, Jack in four suits. Aces are not the highest! Order: â™¥A > â™£10 > â™ 10 > â™¥10 > Queens > Jacks > â™¢A > â™¢10.
setup.dealing: Dealer deals 4 cards to each player (usually in a single round).

rules.objective: Win the majority of points (at least 53 out of 104 available).
rules.gameplay: Dealer deals all 16 cards one at a time (4 each). Player to dealer's left leads. Must follow suit; all trumps count as one suit. Must beat the highest card in the trick if possible. Winner of each trick leads to the next. Four tricks; team with at least 53 of 104 points wins. Tie 52-52: side that announced last double loses, or if no double the old team or lone player loses.
keyRules: Must follow suit; all trumps count as one suit.
Must beat the highest card in the trick if possible.
Winner of each trick leads to the next.
Objective: take at least 53 of 104 card points (A=11, 10=10, Q=3, J=2).
Partnerships: holders of the two black Queens are partners, or declarer plays alone (Wesele, Zolo, Zolo Du).

strategy.basic: Identify your partner! In a Normal Game, watch who plays the black Queens. If you don't have one, your partner is the other person who doesn't play one.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Ten' Flush: Since Tens are worth 10 points and are high trumps, use your top three trumps (â™¥A, â™£10, â™ 10) to 'flush' the remaining Tens out of the opponents' hands as early as possible.
strategy.advanced: Zolo Du (Solo Tout) Detection: If you see someone bid Solo Tout, they almost certainly hold the top three trumps. Your only hope is to hold the 4th top trump (â™¥10) and wait to trap their lead.
tips: Card points in the entire game total exactly 104. Knowing you have 52 points means you only need 1 more to avoid a tie.
A tie (52-52) in some variants means the defenders win; check house rules.
